subject: Re: Post-stratification for improved variance estimates AND

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Post-stratification for improved variance estimates AND
parts:
Hi Alex, list,

Yes, in Distance 6.0 you can use the new systematic design variance
estimators of Fewster et al. (2009) in addition to having a single level
of stratification. These estimators give a much better estimate of true
variance for systematic parallel line transect designs, and as a bonus
the estimate should be much lower if there are strong spatial trends in
density running perpendicular to the lines.

To set the variance estimator, choose the Advanced... button in the
Variance tab of the model definition (assuming you're using CDS or MCDS;
for MRDS the new systematic variance estimators are available in R, but
this is not yet exposed in the interface). Fewster recommends the
overlapping strata estimator (O2) over the non-overlapping on (S2) - see
the paper for details. Note that it is incorrect to try both and choose
the one with the smaller variance estimate!

You didn't say, but I assume you have a systematic parallel line
transect design -- this is the situation the estimators were designed for.

You can specify analysis options for the SpeciesMonth stratum as usual -
nothing is changed there.

Note that it would be incorrect to post-stratify into "good" and and
"poor" end having seen the data and realized that species density is
higher at one end than the other: such things should be decided at the
design stage, not after peeking at the data to reveal density patterns.
If you do it at after looking at the data, you can get a badly
underestimated variance. However, you don't need to do this in any case.

Cheers,

- Len Thomas

Fewster, R.M., S.T. Buckland, K.P. Burnham, D.L. Borchers, P.E. Jupp,
J.L. Laake and L. Thomas. 2009. Estimating the encounter rate variance
in distance sampling. Biometrics 65: 225-236.
Copy available at
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/FewsterBiometrics2009.pdf

--

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Post-stratification for improved variance estimates AND
parts:
Hi Alex. You don't clarify what your existing strata are. If your
design has one set of equally-spaced lines throughout your study area,
then you can ignore existing strata, and pair up lines to get a better
estimate of the systematic variance. If you have different sampling
intensities in each stratum, and sufficient lines per stratum, you could
apply the technique within strata. However, I suspect even there, you
would get a pretty good (better?) estimate if you ignore strata, and
just pair up neighbouring lines throughout the study region.

Incidentally, our paper on getting better estimates of systematic
variances has now appeared:

Fewster, R.M., Buckland, S.T., Burnham, K.P., Borchers, D.L., Jupp,
P.E., Laake, J.L. and Thomas, L. 2009. Estimating the encounter rate
variance in distance sampling. /Biometrics/ *65*, 225-236.


Steve Buckland

> > Hi,
> >
> > I'm working with a dataset from 7 monthly surveys of 2 species of possum.
> >
> > We're using a global detection function, and I've worked out how to get the
> > appropriate individual estimates nicely (a SpeciesMonth stratum).
> >
> > But there is a clear density gradient across the systematically-sampled area
> > -- the two "end lines" are especially poor. I was hoping to use the
> > post-stratification-pairing-lines-up technique to estimate the variance
> > better (the Encounter rate is contributing between 94 and 99% of the variance).
> >
> >
> > Is it possible to use this technique alongside existing strata?
> >
> > Or should I stratify the existing strata into the "poor" end and the "good"
